chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Origins (509-450 BCE)

questions.question: What made the second board of decemvirs notorious?
options: They refused to step down when their term ended
They burned the first ten tables
questions.explanation: The second board, appointed to add two more tables, clung to power past its term. According to tradition, they even had a critic, a soldier and former tribune, killed.
questions.sourceQuote: Its members refused to step down when their term ended, and according to tradition they had a critic, a soldier and former tribune, killed.

questions.question: Who advised the plebeian soldiers to refuse to march in 494 BC?
questions.explanation: The plebeian Lucius Sicinius Vellutus advised the walkout to the Sacred Mount. He was later chosen as one of the early tribunes' colleagues.
questions.sourceQuote: Advised by a plebeian named Lucius Sicinius Vellutus, the plebeian soldiers refused to march.

questions.question: When did the habit of calling plebeians simply the 'lower class' begin?
options: In the late Republic, centuries afterwards
At the founding of the Republic
After the Twelve Tables were published
In the time of the kings
questions.explanation: The label 'lower class' dates only from the late Republic. In fact many plebeians are known to have been wealthy landowners.
questions.sourceQuote: The habit of calling them simply the 'lower class' dates only from the late Republic, centuries afterwards.

questions.question: Why, according to tradition, did the Senate choose Agrippa Menenius Lanatus to negotiate with the seceding plebs?
options: He had written Rome's first laws
He was a former consul the plebs liked
He commanded the army against the Volsci
He was the plebeians' own tribune
questions.explanation: Menenius was a former consul popular with the plebs, sent to talk them round. He used a fable about the body's limbs and belly to argue for cooperation.
questions.sourceQuote: According to tradition, the Senate sent Agrippa Menenius Lanatus, a former consul the plebs liked, to talk them round.

questions.question: Why did meeting by curiae disadvantage the early Plebeian Council?
options: Curiae met only once a year
Curiae could only meet outside the city
It required votes to be unanimous
It kept plebeians dependent on their patrician patrons
questions.explanation: The curiae dated from the time of the kings and tied humbler families to powerful patrician patrons. This also let patricians sway the election of tribunes.
questions.sourceQuote: That kept them dependent on their patrician patrons, powerful men to whom humbler families owed loyalty.

questions.question: Which roles did plebeians fill in the early Roman Republic? (select all that apply)
options: Filling the ranks of the army
questions.explanation: Plebeians, the great majority of citizens, farmed, ran shops and workshops, and made up the army. The consulship and other offices belonged to the patricians.
questions.sourceQuote: They farmed the land, ran the shops and workshops, and filled the ranks of the army.

questions.question: According to Livy, how did the consul Appius respond to the uproar over debt in 495 BC?
options: He issued decrees backing creditors' right to imprison debtors
He handed the case to the pontifices
He created the office of tribune
He gave the officer back his farm
questions.explanation: Instead of offering relief, Appius sided with the creditors. With patricians holding every office, the plebeians could find no remedy inside the system.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead of relief, according to Livy, the consul Appius issued decrees backing creditors' right to imprison debtors.

questions.question: What did Table XI of the Twelve Tables ban?
questions.explanation: Table XI, one of the two supplementary tables, banned patrician-plebeian intermarriage. Table XII covered damage done by slaves.
questions.sourceQuote: Of the two supplementary tables, XI banned marriage between patricians and plebeians, and XII covered damage done by slaves.

questions.question: In Livy's story of the indebted officer, which enemy burned his farm and stole his goods?
questions.explanation: During a war against the Sabines, a hill people north-east of Rome, the enemy burned his farm. Back home he fell into crushing debt and was eventually jailed and whipped.
questions.sourceQuote: During a war against the Sabines, a hill people north-east of Rome, the enemy had burned his farm and stolen his goods.

questions.question: In the view of sceptics like Richard E. Mitchell, where did the story of the conflict come from?
options: Late Republic Romans reading their own class struggles back into the past
questions.explanation: Sceptics argue that Romans of the late Republic, living through violent class struggles, projected those battles onto their distant past. Mitchell argues there was no conflict at all.
questions.sourceQuote: In this view, Romans of the late Republic, living through violent class struggles of their own, read those battles back into their distant past.
